counselling-archaeology-careers.title: Career counselling in archaeology and heritage
counselling-archaeology-careers.subtitle: A private online session on study and career choices
counselling-archaeology-careers.description:
A one-to-one conversation about your next step: which master's or doctoral programmes suit you, how entrance examinations and fieldwork applications work, and what roles exist in museums, survey, conservation and heritage management.

The session is held online at a time agreed with you. Its length and fee are confirmed when you enquire.

details.Scheduling: A time is agreed with you

sakta-ethos-devimahatmya-recording.description: A lecture on how the Devīmāhātmya presents the Goddess, and what the text reveals about the Śākta and tantric traditions that developed around it.

programmes.title: Mehrauli Archaeological Park
programmes.subtitle: A guided heritage walk through ten centuries of building, from the Sultanate to the British period
programmes.description:
The park holds standing remains from the eleventh century to the nineteenth, among them Rajon ki Baoli, the tomb of Balban and the mosque and tomb of Jamali Kamali. An archaeologist shows how masonry, arches and decoration distinguish one period from the next.

The date, start time, pace and language are arranged to suit your group.

details.For: Schools, colleges, companies and the public
details.When: Any day you choose. Early morning is best in the warmer months.
details.Group size: About 10 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.Meeting point: Agreed with you. A map location is shared once the date is confirmed.
details.What to bring: Comfortable shoes, water and a hat. The ground is uneven in places.
details.Entry fees: Monument entry fees, where charged, are not included.

highlights: Rajon ki Baoli, a Lodi-period stepwell with its mosque and tomb
Balban's tomb, with one of the earliest true arches in India
The mosque and tomb of Jamali Kamali, from the first years of Mughal rule
Quli Khan's tomb, which a British official turned into a country house

programmes.title: The Qutb complex
programmes.subtitle: A guided heritage walk through a World Heritage Site, read from its inscriptions and masonry
programmes.description:
The Qutb Minar stands beside a mosque built with reused temple pillars, an iron pillar of the Gupta period and the Alai Darwaza of 1311. The walk uses the inscriptions and the joints in the masonry to trace how the complex grew under successive rulers.

The date, start time, pace and language are arranged to suit your group.

details.For: Schools, colleges, companies and the public
details.When: Any day you choose. Early morning is best in the warmer months.
details.Group size: About 10 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.Meeting point: Agreed with you. A map location is shared once the date is confirmed.
details.What to bring: Comfortable shoes, water and a hat. The ground is uneven in places.
details.Entry fees: Monument entry fees, where charged, are not included.

highlights: The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and its reused temple pillars
The Iron Pillar and its Gupta-period Sanskrit inscription
The Qutb Minar storey by storey, and who built which
The Alai Darwaza, Iltutmish's tomb and the unfinished Alai Minar

programmes.title: Purana Qila
programmes.subtitle: A guided heritage walk around a sixteenth-century fort and the excavations within it
programmes.description:
The fort was built under Humayun and Sher Shah Suri. Excavations inside it since the 1950s have found settlement going back more than two thousand years. The walk covers the walls, gateways and mosque, and what each excavation revealed.

The date, start time, pace and language are arranged to suit your group.

details.When: Any day you choose. Early morning is best in the warmer months.
details.Group size: About 10 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.Meeting point: Agreed with you. A map location is shared once the date is confirmed.
details.What to bring: Comfortable shoes, water and a hat. The ground is uneven in places.
details.Entry fees: Monument entry fees, where charged, are not included.

highlights: The three gateways and the walls of the sixteenth-century fort
The Qila-i-Kuhna mosque and the Sher Mandal
The excavations from the 1950s to the most recent seasons, and what each layer held
How archaeologists date a site lived on for more than two thousand years

programmes.title: Hauz Khas
programmes.subtitle: A guided heritage walk around a fourteenth-century madrasa, tomb and reservoir
programmes.description:
Alauddin Khalji had the reservoir dug for his city of Siri. Firoz Shah Tughlaq later built a madrasa along its edge and his own tomb at the corner. The walk explains how the madrasa functioned and how to recognise Tughlaq architecture.

The date, start time, pace and language are arranged to suit your group.

details.For: Schools, colleges, companies and the public
details.When: Any day you choose. Early morning is best in the warmer months.
details.Group size: About 10 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.Meeting point: Agreed with you. A map location is shared once the date is confirmed.
details.What to bring: Comfortable shoes, water and a hat. The ground is uneven in places.
details.Entry fees: Monument entry fees, where charged, are not included.

highlights: The reservoir Alauddin Khalji had dug for his city of Siri
Firoz Shah Tughlaq's madrasa, hall by hall
Firoz Shah's tomb and the pavilions in the garden
How to recognise Tughlaq building: sloping walls, plain stone, little ornament

programmes.title: Museum gallery study
programmes.subtitle: A guided museum visit that studies one gallery in depth, object by object
programmes.description:
Rather than a rapid tour of a whole museum, this visit concentrates on a single gallery chosen with you. An archaeologist takes the group through about a dozen objects: what each is, how it was made and found, and what it tells us.

The gallery, date, pace and language are arranged to suit your group.
programmes.venue: A Delhi museum chosen with you

details.For: Schools, colleges, companies and the public
details.When: Any day the museum is open. Its weekly closing day is checked before the date is fixed.
details.Group size: About 10 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.Meeting point: Agreed with you. A map location is shared once the date is confirmed.
details.Entry fees: Museum entry fees are not included.

highlights: One gallery, chosen with you beforehand
About a dozen objects, each looked at slowly
How to read a museum label, and what it leaves out
Questions you can carry into any other gallery

programmes.title: Culture and heritage
programmes.subtitle: An illustrated lecture on tangible and intangible heritage, and on who protects it
programmes.description:
The lecture explains what counts as culture and what counts as heritage, and how the two differ. It works through tangible and intangible heritage with Indian examples, then looks at the institutions and communities that protect it, from UNESCO and the Archaeological Survey of India to the people who live beside a monument.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: Culture and heritage: the difference, with Indian examples
Tangible and intangible heritage
Who protects heritage: UNESCO, the Archaeological Survey of India and local communities
Time for the group's own questions

programmes.title: Archaeology in practice
programmes.subtitle: An illustrated lecture on how sites are found, excavated, recorded and cared for
programmes.description:
The lecture follows an archaeological site from the first survey to the museum shelf: how a site is located, how a trench is laid out and recorded, what happens to finds in the laboratory, and what becomes of a site once excavation ends.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: How sites are found
How a trench is laid out, dug and recorded
What happens to finds in the laboratory
What becomes of a site after the dig

programmes.title: From stone tools to the first villages
programmes.subtitle: An illustrated lecture on human origins and the Stone Age in South Asia
programmes.description:
The lecture traces how early people lived in the subcontinent through the tools they left behind, from handaxes to microliths to the first farming settlements, using photographs of excavated material.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: The oldest stone tools found in the subcontinent
Handaxes, flake tools and microliths: what changed and why
The first farming villages
How archaeologists date finds this old

programmes.title: The first cities: the Indus and its contemporaries
programmes.subtitle: An illustrated lecture comparing the Indus cities with Mesopotamia, Egypt and early China
programmes.description:
The lecture examines what made a city more than four thousand years ago: planning, drainage, standard weights, seals and trade. Setting the Harappan cities beside their contemporaries shows what the early civilisations shared and what was distinctive to the Indus.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: What makes a settlement a city
Planning, drains, weights and seals in the Indus cities
Mesopotamia, Egypt and early China beside the Indus
The Indus script, which no one has yet read

programmes.title: India's scripts: from Brāhmī to Śāradā
programmes.subtitle: An illustrated lecture, with a reading demonstration, on the Brāhmī family of scripts
programmes.description:
Most scripts used in India today descend from Brāhmī, the script of most of Aśoka's edicts. The lecture traces that family, reads a line of an edict with the audience, and shows how epigraphists date an inscription from the shapes of its letters.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: Brāhmī, the script of most of Aśoka's edicts
How Brāhmī grew into the scripts of north and south India
A line of an edict, read together
Dating an inscription from the shape of its letters

programmes.title: Reading a temple
programmes.subtitle: A single illustrated lecture on the Nāgara, Drāviḍa and Vesara traditions
programmes.description:
A plan, an elevation and a small set of terms are enough to begin reading a temple. The lecture compares the northern, southern and Deccan traditions through photographs and drawings. For a fuller treatment, see the four-session course on Indian temple architecture.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: The parts of a temple, from gateway to sanctum
Nāgara, Drāviḍa and Vesara: how to tell them apart
Reading a plan and an elevation
Examples from north India, the south and the Deccan

programmes.title: India's linguistic heritage
programmes.subtitle: An illustrated lecture on the language families of the subcontinent and their history
programmes.description:
India's languages belong to several families that have influenced one another for thousands of years. The lecture maps those families, explains how linguists reconstruct their history, and considers what is lost when a language ceases to be spoken.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: The language families of India: Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austroasiatic, Tibeto-Burman and others
How neighbouring languages borrow from one another
How linguists reconstruct a language's history
Endangered languages, and what is lost with them

programmes.title: Rock art of India
programmes.subtitle: An illustrated lecture on India's painted shelters and rock engravings
programmes.description:
India has one of the world's largest bodies of rock art, from the painted shelters of Bhimbetka to the engravings of the Konkan coast. The lecture looks at what the images depict, how they are dated, and how researchers document them before they fade.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: The painted shelters of Bhimbetka and central India
The rock engravings of the Konkan coast
How rock art is dated
How it is recorded and protected

programmes.title: The Devīmāhātmya: the Goddess in text and image
programmes.subtitle: An illustrated lecture on the Devīmāhātmya and the Śākta tradition
programmes.description:
The Devīmāhātmya is the best-known Sanskrit text on the Goddess and is still recited during Navarātri. The lecture reads key passages in translation and sets them beside sculpture and painting to show how the Śākta tradition took shape.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: Where the text sits in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa
Its three episodes: Madhu and Kaiṭabha, Mahiṣāsura, Śumbha and Niśumbha
Key passages read in translation
The Goddess in sculpture and painting

programmes.title: Careers in archaeology, museums and heritage
programmes.subtitle: A guidance lecture for students choosing what to study
programmes.description:
The lecture sets out what the work involves, which degrees lead to it and where the employment is. Students leave with an outline of courses, entrance routes and first steps, and time is given to their own questions.

Length, level and language are agreed with you. The lecture can be given online or at your venue, for a single class, a department or a whole organisation.

details.When: Any date you choose, daytime or evening.
details.Group size: About 25 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.You arrange: At your venue, a room with a screen or projector. Online, nothing; the link is sent to you.

highlights: What the work is, in the field, the museum and the archive
Which degrees lead to it, and how to get in
Where the jobs are
The students' own questions

programmes.title: Mock excavation
programmes.subtitle: A hands-on workshop in which students excavate and record a prepared trench
programmes.description:
A trench is prepared in advance with layers and planted finds. Students excavate it with real tools, record each find and its position, and then interpret what happened at the site.

All materials are provided. The session is adapted to your space, your timetable and the age of the participants.
programmes.venue: Your campus, outdoors or in sand trays

details.When: Any date you choose.
details.Group size: About 20 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.We provide: All materials, for the confirmed number of participants.
details.You arrange: An open area of ground, or a room if sand trays are used.

highlights: Laying out a trench and digging it layer by layer
Recording each find and where it lay
Working out, as a team, what happened at the site

programmes.title: Pottery: making and identification
programmes.subtitle: A hands-on workshop in shaping pottery and in sorting sherds as archaeologists do
programmes.description:
Pottery is the most common find on an excavation. Participants shape a vessel by hand, then sort replica sherds by fabric, form and decoration, as archaeologists do in the field.

All materials are provided. The session is adapted to your space, your timetable and the age of the participants.

details.When: Any date you choose.
details.Group size: About 20 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.We provide: All materials, for the confirmed number of participants.
details.You arrange: A room or open space with tables. Exact requirements are confirmed once the group is known.

highlights: Shaping a pot by hand
Sorting sherds by fabric, form and decoration
What pottery tells an archaeologist about date and daily life

programmes.title: Identifying sculpture
programmes.subtitle: A half-day workshop combining a short lecture, a gallery or temple visit and a quiz
programmes.description:
After a short illustrated lecture on how figures are identified, participants study sculpture in a museum gallery or at a temple, identify figures from their attributes and dress, and finish with a quiz.

All materials are provided. The session is adapted to your space, your timetable and the age of the participants.
programmes.venue: A museum or temple near you

details.When: Any date you choose.
details.Group size: About 20 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.We provide: All materials, for the confirmed number of participants.
details.You arrange: A room with a screen for the lecture. Entry fees for the visit, where charged, are not included.

highlights: A short illustrated talk on how figures are identified
Study in a gallery or at a temple: what each figure holds and wears
A quiz to finish

programmes.title: Introduction to Brāhmī script
programmes.subtitle: A hands-on workshop in reading and writing the script of Aśoka's edicts
programmes.description:
Brāhmī is more than two thousand years old and can be learnt to a basic level in a single session. Participants learn the letters, write their own names, and read a few words from an Aśokan edict.

All materials are provided. The session is adapted to your space, your timetable and the age of the participants.

Writing your own name
Reading a few words from an Aśokan edict

programmes.title: Archaeological documentation
programmes.subtitle: A hands-on workshop in recording sites and objects to a professional standard
programmes.description:
A find without a record is only an old object. Participants complete a context sheet, draw and photograph an object to scale, and write a catalogue entry, using the formats applied in field and museum practice.

All materials are provided. The session is adapted to your space, your timetable and the age of the participants.

details.When: Any date you choose.
details.Group size: About 20 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.We provide: All materials, for the confirmed number of participants.
details.You arrange: A room with tables and a screen.

highlights: Filling in a context sheet
Drawing and photographing an object to scale
Writing a catalogue entry

programmes.title: Preventive conservation
programmes.subtitle: A one- or two-day workshop on caring for paper, textiles and metal
programmes.description:
Most damage to a collection is caused by light, damp, pests and handling, and much of it can be prevented at little cost. A conservator shows how to assess, store and handle paper, textiles and metal, with practice on sample materials.

All materials are provided. The session is adapted to your space, your timetable and the age of the participants.

details.For: Colleges, museums, archives and company collections
details.When: Any date you choose.
details.Group size: About 20 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.We provide: All materials, for the confirmed number of participants.
details.You arrange: A room with tables and a screen.

highlights: What damages a collection: light, damp, pests and handling
Assessing the condition of an object
Storing and handling paper, textiles and metal
Practice on sample materials

programmes.title: Stone tools: making and classification
programmes.subtitle: A hands-on workshop on how prehistoric stone tools were made, used and classified
programmes.description:
A prehistorian demonstrates how stone tools were struck and what the scars on them reveal. Participants sort tool types, handle replicas and learn the first steps of lithic analysis.

All materials are provided. The session is adapted to your space, your timetable and the age of the participants.

details.Group size: About 20 is suggested. Smaller and larger groups are welcome.
details.We provide: All materials, for the confirmed number of participants.
details.You arrange: A room with tables and a screen.

highlights: A demonstration of how stone tools were struck
Reading the scars on a tool
Sorting tool types and handling replicas

programmes.title: Team excavation challenge
programmes.subtitle: A half-day hands-on workshop for workplace teams
programmes.description:
Teams excavate, record and interpret a prepared trench, then present their reading of the evidence. The exercise rewards careful observation and clear reporting rather than speed.

All materials are provided. The session is adapted to your space, your timetable and the age of the participants.
programmes.venue: Your office or an offsite venue

details.When: Any date you choose.

They record their finds as they go
Each team presents its reading of the evidence
Careful observation and clear reporting win, not speed

programmes.title: Introductory Prakrit
programmes.subtitle: An online course of six sessions in Prakrit grammar and reading
programmes.description:
Prakrit was the everyday speech of much of ancient India and the language of Aśoka's edicts. The course covers the essentials of grammar, with guided reading of short passages.

The course is run for your batch on dates you choose. Timings, pace and assessment are agreed before it begins.

Guided reading of short passages
Where Prakrit is found: inscriptions, drama and Jain texts

programmes.title: Introductory Pali
programmes.subtitle: An online course in Pali pronunciation, grammar and reading
programmes.description:
Pali is the language of the Theravāda Buddhist canon. The course covers pronunciation, basic grammar and the reading of short passages, and ends with an optional assessment.

The course is run for your batch on dates you choose. Timings, pace and assessment are agreed before it begins.

Reading short passages

programmes.title: Reading Śāradā script
programmes.subtitle: An online course of about ten sessions in reading Śāradā manuscripts
programmes.description:
Śāradā was the principal script of Kashmir for centuries, and many manuscripts from the region are written in it. Participants learn the alphabet, conjuncts and numerals, practise transliteration, and read from manuscript pages.

The course is run for your batch on dates you choose. Timings, pace and assessment are agreed before it begins.

Practice in transliteration
Reading from manuscript pages

programmes.title: Understanding Indian temple architecture
programmes.subtitle: An online course of four sessions on the forms and development of the Indian temple
programmes.description:
An introduction to the parts of a temple, the regional styles and their chronology, and the methods scholars use to study architecture. A certificate of completion can be issued.

programmes.title: Remote sensing in archaeology and heritage management
programmes.subtitle: A three-month online certificate course, taught in live weekend sessions
programmes.description:
The course covers how satellite imagery, aerial photographs and mapping software are used to find, map and monitor sites. Each live session is recorded for participants who miss it.

The course is run for your batch on dates you choose. Timings, pace and assessment are agreed before it begins.

programmes.title: Martial arts and society
programmes.subtitle: An online course of three sessions on wrestling and combat in Indian history
programmes.description:
The course examines what sculpture, texts and living traditions reveal about wrestling and combat sports in India, and what they meant to those who practised and patronised them.

The course is run for your batch on dates you choose. Timings, pace and assessment are agreed before it begins.

Traditions that are still practised
What these sports meant to those who practised and paid for them

programmes.title: Museum field school: documentation and conservation
programmes.subtitle: A week-long field school of supervised work on a museum collection
programmes.description:
Participants document, clean and rehouse objects from a museum collection under the supervision of conservators and documentation specialists, with daily laboratory sessions, lectures and visits to nearby sites. It is suited to students of conservation, museology, archaeology and related subjects.

Dates, location and syllabus are agreed with your institution. A day-by-day plan and a quotation are shared before you commit.

Cleaning and rehousing them under supervision
Daily laboratory sessions and lectures
Visits to nearby sites

programmes.title: Prehistory field school
programmes.subtitle: A three-day field school in survey, stone tools, rock art and megaliths
programmes.description:
A field introduction to prehistory: reading the local landscape, locating and classifying stone tools, documenting rock art and megaliths, and taking samples.
